A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the third-order non-linear response of a semiconductor is the result of three distinct one-electron mechanisms, and that the relative importance of each is determined by the frequency of the incident light pulse, the carrier density and the pulse rise time.

the non-linear response can be divided into three distinct regimes, each of which has a different physical origin and a different frequency dependence, and that the transition from one regime to the next can be explained in terms of changes in the dephasing rate of the electronic transition.

the intensity-dependent shift in the energy levels of a two-level system is a fundamental mechanism for non-linear optical phenomena, and that the non-linear refractive index of a semiconductor is a direct consequence of the intensity-dependence of the energy levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the non-linear refraction is a consequence of the motion of the electrons and holes in their effective mass band structure, and not a consequence of any particular mechanism, such as the virtual transition or band filling.
the three main mechanisms for non-linear refractive index are intimately related to each other and that they are all a consequence of the same underlying physics, namely the optical Stark effect.
the intensity-dependent index of refraction of a semiconductor is the consequence of a single mechanism, namely the motion of free electrons and holes in the non-parablic band.
